items.title: Perseverance confirms complex organic carbon just under the skin of ancient Martian rock
items.why: Organics on Mars are not new by themselves; the interesting part is that these held up just beneath a weathered surface, and that similar finds elsewhere on the planet suggest this is a pattern rather than one lucky rock. Nobody is claiming life, and the careful phrasing is the sign of a team that knows the sample-return question hangs on exactly this sort of result.
items.summary: NASA's Perseverance rover has confirmed complex organic carbon preserved a little below the surface of old Martian rocks. Combined with comparable detections far away on Mars, the result hints that life's chemical building blocks may once have been common across the planet, though it says nothing yet about whether anything used them.

items.title: Euclid's first big data release, a down payment on a 3D map of the dark universe
items.why: Survey telescopes are the slow-cooked dishes of astronomy: years of patient tiling before the cosmology comes out of the oven. This first release is the bit where the rest of us get to look at the pictures, and with a 600-megapixel camera the pictures are very much worth looking at.
items.summary: ESA's Euclid space telescope has published its first large batch of survey data. The mission is building the biggest three-dimensional map of the universe yet, aimed at pinning down dark energy and dark matter, and the release comes with a set of showcase images from its wide-field camera.

items.title: This year's bird name changes, lumps and splits, from willets to wrens
items.why: Every year the taxonomists giveth and the taxonomists taketh away, and every year listers quietly recount. Audubon's annual roundup is the friendly version of the checklist supplement: which birds just became two, which two turned out to be one, and why the genetics changed minds.
items.summary: Audubon walks through this year's official changes to bird names and species boundaries. As research on relationships between birds advances, some former species are split into several, others are lumped together, and a few get new names; willets, warblers and wrens are among the groups affected this time.

items.title: LWN on the second half of the record-breaking Linux 7.4 merge window
items.why: The headline number is a record, but the more telling line is LWN's observation that bug fixes seem to be crowding out features. Elsewhere, DAMON keeps sprouting knobs, including hugetlb access tracking that VM hosts will care about, and Super-H quietly sheds NUMA and sparse memory support that was buying it all of 128KB.
items.summary: The second part of LWN's merge-window report covers the changes that landed in Linux 7.4 after its first article, out of a record total of more than 18,500 non-merge changesets. Highlights include new DAMON filters and hugetlb access tracking, invertible DAMON target metrics, and the removal of NUMA and sparse-memory support from the Super-H architecture.

items.title: A tiny JIT that renders proportional bitmap text on an RP2350
items.why: Generating machine code on the fly to draw a string is the kind of trick that would have made a demoscener nod approvingly in 1988, and here it serves an entirely sensible goal: early-Mac-style proportional, kerned bitmap fonts on a microcontroller that would rather you used a fixed character grid. The history detour on font ROMs versus framebuffers is a nice bonus.
items.summary: Working on vic-2350, a reimagined 1980s home computer built on an RP2350 microcontroller board, the author wanted crisp bitmap fonts with proportional spacing and kerning rather than fixed character cells. The post explains how a small just-in-time compiler generates optimised code per string so it can be drawn fast enough while racing the display beam.

items.title: A Nixie clock that counts down to the next bus instead of telling the time
items.why: Nixie tubes are wasted on the time of day; everybody already has a dozen clocks. Reflashing the board's firmware with an ST-LINK and handing the transit lookup to a Raspberry Pi is the right division of labour, and the result is a gadget that answers the only question that matters at seven in the morning.
items.summary: Justin Scott took an off-the-shelf two-digit Nixie clock board, built it a handsome enclosure, then hacked its firmware so it displays the minutes until the next bus at his local stop. A Raspberry Pi fetches the schedule and passes the countdown to the clock over a serial link.

items.title: Nineteenth-century ikat textiles from Bukhara
items.why: Ikat is one of those techniques that sounds impossible when explained: the pattern is dyed into the threads before anything is woven, which is why the edges of each shape blur and shimmer. The Public Domain Review's gallery is a good place to let the colours do the talking.
items.summary: A Public Domain Review collection of vivid ikat textiles from nineteenth-century Central Asia, centred on Bukhara, the old Timurid-era trading city. In ikat the threads are resist-dyed before weaving, giving the bold, slightly feathered patterns these cloths are known for.

items.title: Truxton, New York, and its three tributes to Little Napoleon, John McGraw
items.why: A village of a few hundred people honouring its most famous son with a monument, a ballfield, and a sign commemorating the ballgame that paid for the monument is pure small-town America, and rather sweet. McGraw managed the New York Giants for three decades, so the stakes for local pride were high.
items.summary: In the central New York village of Truxton, where baseball manager John J. McGraw was born in 1873, three linked sites remember him: a stone monument, a baseball field named after him, and a marker for the game played there that raised the money for the memorial. The entry also sketches the McGraw family's hard early years in the town.

items.title: Trouble the Water, part two: how spirituals turned into gospel after emancipation
items.why: No Depression is funding long-form reporting on the foundations of roots music, and this second chapter picks up the story where freedom arrives and the music has to find new rooms to live in. Slow reading, in the best sense, and a reminder of how much of the string-band and songwriter world stands on this ground.
items.summary: The second instalment of Santi Elijah Holley's No Depression fellowship series follows African American sacred music from the end of the Civil War onward, tracing how the spirituals sung under slavery developed into gospel. It continues his earlier chapter on spirituals as a founding form of American roots music.

items.title: The index to Thomas Browne's collected works, a cabinet of curiosities in alphabetical order
items.why: An index is usually where curiosity goes to be filed and forgotten, but the 1835 index to Browne's works reads like a found poem by a man who wanted to know everything, from ostriches digesting iron to Greek cavalry in quincunx formation. A short one, and a perfect idle-moment read.
items.summary: Futility Closet shares entries from the index to the 1835 edition of the works of Sir Thomas Browne, the seventeenth-century English physician and polymath. The entries jump from apes and bay leaves to crocodiles that supposedly never stop growing, showing how wide his interests ran.

items.title: A possible new dwarf planet turns up in Rubin data, on a roughly 280-year orbit
items.why: Rubin was built to drown astronomers in faint moving dots, and here is the payoff: out of two thousand-odd new small bodies, one that looked suspiciously large. The nice part of the story is the restraint, a researcher who has been burned before keeping his hopes in check while the numbers firm up. Dwarf-planet status is a high bar, but the odds look better than usual.
items.summary: Matthew Holman and Kevin Napier of the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory were combing Vera C. Rubin Observatory data with their own software when one distant object stood out for its apparent size. It circles the Sun roughly once every 280 years, and it may qualify as a new dwarf planet in the outer solar system.

items.title: Bennu's sample and the Murchison meteorite tell different stories about the same amino acid
items.why: OSIRIS-REx keeps paying out years after it dropped its capsule in the Utah desert. The clever bit here is the measurement itself: isotopic differences between individual atoms inside one molecule, which is the kind of forensic resolution that lets you ask where in the early solar system a building block of life was cooked.
items.summary: Researchers measured the amino acid beta-alanine in material returned from asteroid Bennu and in the Murchison meteorite, comparing isotopes not just molecule by molecule but atom by atom within the molecule. The results suggest the same prebiotic ingredients formed under different conditions in different parts of the young protoplanetary disk.

items.title: LEGO marks fifty years of Star Wars with a wave of 2027 sets
items.why: Fifty years of Star Wars is a scary number for anyone who remembers the first one in a cinema, and LEGO, which let some recent anniversaries slide by quietly, has decided this one gets the full treatment. The Brothers Brick has the box shots and the first look; the fun is spotting which corners of the saga got the brick-built nod.
items.summary: The Brothers Brick reports on seven new LEGO Star Wars sets due in the new year to celebrate the franchise's 50th anniversary in 2027, with images and details of what is in each box.

items.title: Let's write a PostScript interpreter, one human-scale piece at a time
items.why: The opening argument is the late-90s spirit in one line: the most trustworthy languages are the ones a single person could write from scratch. PostScript is a perfect specimen, a stack machine that happens to draw, and watching a working subset come together in a single post is the sort of thing that makes you want to open an editor on a Friday night.
items.summary: A walkthrough of building an interpreter for an interesting subset of PostScript, the stack-based page description language. Error handling and many features are simplified away, but every example is valid PostScript, and the post makes the case for small languages a single person can understand completely.

items.title: The Secret of Monkey Island, all 13 versions side by side
items.why: This is archival work done with real care: the same twelve moments captured in every release, scaled with square-pixel honesty and aspect correction, so the only thing that changes when you switch is the machine. A small museum of late-80s and early-90s home computing told through one pirate game, and a wildcard for anyone who spent too long on Melee Island.
items.summary: A browsable comparison of all thirteen releases of LucasArts' The Secret of Monkey Island, from Atari ST monochrome to PC 16-colour and beyond. Each version is shown at the same twelve points in the game, captured in ScummVM or an Atari ST emulator and scaled to preserve the original pixel shapes.

items.title: Photon: how Google joined continuous streams exactly once, via The Morning Paper
items.why: Exactly-once semantics, datacenter-level fault tolerance, unordered streams and a primary stream that shows up late: Photon took on the whole list at once, and it did so on the system that books Google's ad revenue, so failure was not theoretical. Adrian Colyer's write-up is a good way back into a paper that shaped a lot of later streaming work.
items.summary: An archive post from The Morning Paper on Google's 2013 Photon paper, which describes a system for continuously joining multiple data streams with exactly-once guarantees, tolerance of whole-datacenter failures, high scale and low latency, even when events arrive out of order or the primary stream is delayed.

items.title: Winter feeding for the birds that stay behind
items.why: When the migrants clear out, the backyard cast that remains is a familiar one for anyone birding in South or Southeast Asia: sparrows, doves, bulbuls and mynas. A gentle, practical piece from a backyard feeder in Pakistan about paying attention to the residents once the visitors have gone.
items.summary: Faisal Rehman, a bird-feeding enthusiast in Pakistan, writes about how his backyard changes after winter migrants leave and the resident House Sparrows, Laughing Doves, bulbuls and mynas take centre stage again, with practical tips on feeding them through the season.

items.title: Edward S. Curtis photographs a Hupa fisherman on the Trinity River, around 1923
items.why: Curtis spent decades documenting Native American life, and this one is a quiet image: a single man on a midstream rock, spear ready, in a haze of smoke. It is a fine way into the Hupa, who have fished salmon on that river for a thousand years and still hold their ancestral valley today.
items.summary: Today's Wikipedia picture of the day is Edward S. Curtis's photograph titled A Smoky Day at the Sugar Bowl, showing a Hupa man standing on a rock in the Trinity River with a fishing spear. The Hupa of northwestern California traditionally relied on salmon, acorns and basketry, and most belong to the Hoopa Valley Tribe today.

items.title: The tar pits on Adams Hill at Fort Sill, Oklahoma
items.why: Tar pits are rarer than you might think, and the famous one in Los Angeles hogs the attention. This modest Oklahoma version, on the grounds of an Army post, has a long human history attached, from early explorers noting it to local Native Americans using the stuff on their horses' saddle sores.
items.summary: Where a gap in the impermeable rock lets oil seep to the surface in southwest Oklahoma, the lighter parts evaporate and leave asphalt behind. The resulting tar pits sit on Fort Sill near Lawton, are among only a few in the world, and were known to early explorers and to local tribes, who used the tar as a remedy for horses.

items.title: The Baltimore Science Fiction Society's little purple book box passes 5,000 books
items.why: Fandom at its most neighbourly: no awards drama, no discourse, just a club keeping a purple box in East Baltimore full of books. Five thousand handed out is a lot of chances for some kid to pick up their first Asimov.
items.summary: A Little Free Library box in East Baltimore, maintained by the Baltimore Science Fiction Society, reached a milestone in October of more than 5,000 books given away to the neighbourhood.

items.title: Nyana rooiwalensis, a new early sauropodomorph from South Africa's Late Triassic
items.why: Before the sauropods got enormous, their ancestors were modest, lightly built animals, and decent skulls from that stage are rare enough that each one counts. This one comes out of the Elliot Formation in the Eastern Cape, a rich Triassic graveyard that keeps handing over relatives of Massospondylus. Worth a look for where it sits on the family tree rather than for size.
items.summary: Palaeontologists have described a new species of early sauropodomorph, the group that later produced the giant long-necked dinosaurs, from a skull found in the Late Triassic rocks of South Africa's Eastern Cape. Skulls from this early stage of the lineage are scarce, so the find helps fill in how the group diversified in southern Gondwana.

items.title: Harris's Hawks, the raptors that hunt as a pack
items.why: Most raptors are loners, which is what makes Harris's Hawk the odd one out: family groups hunt together, flushing and cornering prey in relays, and sometimes stand on each other's backs for a better view. A desert field note from Arizona is a nice reminder that cooperation evolved in some unlikely corners of the bird world.
items.summary: An Audubon Southwest writer describes encountering Harris's Hawks on a walk through the Sonoran Desert and explains the species' social life. Unusually for birds of prey, these hawks live and hunt in cooperative groups, working together to take prey in the open desert.

items.title: A small Nordic cabin on the water, in plate-built walls and seamless rockwork
items.why: Pepijn Kuyvenhoven's cabin is the quiet kind of MOC that rewards a long look: walls built up from plates and tiles rather than bricks, and rockwork that slides into the water without an obvious seam. No starships, no castles, just very good technique applied to somewhere you'd want to sit with a coffee.
items.summary: Builder Pepijn Kuyvenhoven has made a LEGO model of a modest Scandinavian house perched by the water. The Brothers Brick highlights the walls assembled from layered plates and tiles and the natural-looking rock shoreline that blends into the water.

items.title: The Dodder Rhino, a life-size bronze that turned up in a Dublin river and nobody claimed
items.why: A full-size bronze rhinoceros appearing on a plinth mid-river in 2002, with no plaque, no artist and no confession, is exactly the kind of civic mystery Dublin does well. The local pub denied all involvement and then ran a contest to name it, which is the correct response. One for the list if you ever walk the Dodder near Milltown.
items.summary: In the River Dodder near Classon's Bridge in Milltown, Dublin, stands a realistic life-size bronze rhino on a plinth. It appeared in 2002 without any explanation of who made it or put it there, and it has since become an odd local landmark adopted by the neighbourhood.

items.title: Earth may have made its own oceans, cooked up from rock and hydrogen
items.why: The textbook story has comets and asteroids delivering Earth's water by mail order. This experiment suggests the young planet could have brewed its own, fast, by letting hot rocky pebbles react with a hydrogen-rich atmosphere. If it holds, water stops being a lucky accident and becomes a standard feature of rocky planets, which is good news for anyone counting habitable worlds.
items.summary: Researchers found that rocky pebbles exposed to hydrogen at very high temperatures produce water within minutes. Scaled up to the forming Earth, the process could have generated many oceans' worth of water in the early atmosphere, offering an alternative to the idea that water was mostly delivered by impacts.

items.title: Two-phase commit as R* built it, via The Morning Paper
items.why: Mohan and colleagues' 1986 R* paper is where two-phase commit stopped being a whiteboard sketch and got serious about logging and message costs, and where Presumed Abort and Presumed Commit came from. Adrian Colyer's walk-through, part of his Redbook series, is a tidy refresher on why every forced log write in the protocol is there.
items.summary: An archive post from The Morning Paper reviewing the R* distributed database's transaction management paper. It covers the basic coordinator-and-subordinates two-phase commit protocol, how it behaves under site and link failures, and the paper's focus on minimising log writes and messages in the common no-failure case.

items.title: openQ4 brings Quake 4's never-released expansion back from the dead
items.why: Raven and Ritual built a Quake 4 expansion that never shipped; someone recovered it, and an open-source engine replacement now plays it alongside the original campaign on Linux and the Steam Deck. That's the id tradition at its best: the code outlives the publisher's plans, and hobbyists keep the lights on.
items.summary: openQ4 is a free, open-source engine and game-code replacement for Quake 4. Its new release can run the recovered, previously unreleased expansion next to the main campaign, with players supplying the game files, and adds better shadows, a rebuilt interface, Vulkan on Windows, improved bots and an experimental Android build.

items.title: A map of New England places out-of-towners keep mispronouncing
items.why: Worcester, Leominster, Quincy, Peabody: New England's place names are a long-running entrance exam for visitors. Maxwell Howe's map for the 30 Day Map Challenge sets them out, and the best part is the locals immediately arguing over whether dropped R's count as pronunciation or just accent. Concord, for the record, is not the airplane.
items.summary: Made for the 30 Day Map Challenge, Maxwell Howe's map marks New England towns whose names commonly trip up outsiders, with phonetic guides. Readers have pushed back on some entries, debating where correct pronunciation ends and the regional non-rhotic accent begins.

items.title: The Golden Gun's corkscrew car jump was worked out on a computer in 1974
items.why: The spiral jump over a broken bridge in The Man With The Golden Gun looks like pure stunt-driver nerve, but it was simulated first, with Euler's equations of rigid-body motion, on a 1970s computer. A lovely early case of numerical modelling getting a credit it never received on screen.
items.summary: The famous barrel-roll car jump in the 1974 Bond film was planned with computer simulation beforehand. An engineer took detailed measurements of the car and ramps and modelled the stunt using rigid-body equations dating back to Leonhard Euler.

items.title: Achilles' shield, drawn from Homer's description by Quatremère de Quincy in 1814
items.why: Homer describes the shield Hephaestus forged in such detail, cities, harvests, dances, the encircling ocean, that artists have treated it as a set of build instructions for nearly two thousand years. This 1814 reconstruction by a French architectural theorist is a fine example of the genre: part archaeology, part fan art.
items.summary: Futility Closet shares a drawing of the shield of Achilles made in 1814 by the French architectural theorist Quatremère de Quincy. It is one of many attempts over the centuries to reconstruct the shield from its lengthy description in the Iliad.

items.title: Caitlin Canty sits in with The Suitcase Junket at ZenBarn in Vermont
items.why: Any Caitlin Canty sighting goes straight in, and this one comes with a bonus: Matt Lorenz's Suitcase Junket, the one-man band who plays guitar, kick drum and a junk pile of percussion all at once. Canty's unhurried, smoky songwriting next to that racket should make for a very good night in a Waterbury barn.
items.summary: A Vermont paper lists an upcoming Suitcase Junket show at ZenBarn, the farm-to-table music venue in Waterbury, with Caitlin Canty billed as special guest. The Suitcase Junket is the stage name of Matt Lorenz, a New England roots act known for playing several instruments at once.

items.title: The first land animals had stiff necks, and that changes the story of why necks evolved
items.why: Not dinosaurs strictly, but the ancestors of everything with a neck, dinosaurs very much included. The textbook idea was that necks evolved so early tetrapods could swivel their heads; the new work says those first necks barely bent at all. Turns out the neck may be a side effect of learning to walk on front legs, which is the kind of plot twist palaeontology does best.
items.summary: Researchers studying the earliest four-limbed animals to move onto land, around 380 million years ago, found their necks were surprisingly rigid. Rather than evolving for head movement, the neck may have emerged as part of the body reorganisation that let these animals push themselves along with their forelimbs.

items.title: Parker Solar Probe finds the solar wind's magnetic twists flip direction at the smallest scales
items.why: Turbulence is famously the last unsolved problem of classical physics, and the solar wind is turbulence on a heroic scale. Parker, skimming closer to the Sun than anything we have built, found that the twist of the magnetic fluctuations reverses once you zoom in far enough. Odd-looking, tidy patterns inside chaos are the best kind of clue.
items.summary: Data from NASA's Parker Solar Probe show that turbulent magnetic fields in the solar wind reverse their sense of rotation when examined at very small scales. The pattern offers a new handle on how energy cascades through the solar wind, which matters for understanding solar activity and forecasting geomagnetic storms.

items.title: Hubble studies a 93-billion-mile dust cloud that may be debris from colliding worlds
items.why: A dark, fluffy smear of dust a thousand times the Earth-Sun distance long is not something you expect to find just hanging about. The leading idea is that it is the wreckage of large planetary bodies smashing together, which would make it a rare look at the messy demolition-derby phase of building a planetary system.
items.summary: New Hubble observations add detail to a long, dark cloud of fine dust stretching some 93 billion miles. Astronomers suggest it may have formed in a collision between massive planetary bodies, and its structure challenges earlier assumptions about what the object is and how such systems form.

items.title: Studprint: a working 3D printer that is 92 percent LEGO, leadscrews included
items.why: Plenty of builds use LEGO for a frame or a bed; Adam Turaj went the whole way and made the motion system out of LEGO too, leadscrews and all. Nobody is claiming it prints fast or big, and that is rather the point. It is the brick equivalent of building a computer out of relays because you can.
items.summary: Hacker Adam Turaj built Studprint, a 3D printer made almost entirely from LEGO parts, including the leadscrews that drive its axes. It is not a high-performance machine, but it does print, and the write-up covers how far the bricks could be pushed before non-LEGO parts became unavoidable.

items.title: Elite, the 1984 space-trading classic, finally lands on the Commodore PET
items.why: Forty-odd years after BBC Micro owners got to fly Cobras and PET owners got to feel envious, David Given has ported Elite to the PET. Same 6502, slower clock, block graphics instead of wireframes, and 32K of memory to squeeze it into. Exactly the sort of gloriously unnecessary labour of love that keeps old machines alive.
items.summary: David Given has ported Elite, the groundbreaking open-world space game originally written for the BBC Micro, to the Commodore PET. The PET shares the BBC's 6502 processor but runs slower and only has character-block graphics, so the port renders the game's ships in chunky PETSCII and needs a 32K machine.

items.title: Plumbers 2026: how AWS copes with the kernel CVE flood
items.why: Since the kernel became its own CVE numbering authority, the CVE count has gone from a trickle to a firehose, and the downstream side of that story has had little airtime. Corbet's write-up of the Plumbers talk is the view from people who have to keep a fleet patched: the run-current-kernels advice mostly works, with the interesting part being the 'mostly'.
items.summary: LWN reports on a Linux Plumbers Conference session in which two AWS engineers described how a large kernel user handles the flood of CVE assignments. They found that tracking current stable kernels largely holds up, but discussed where it breaks down and what operators actually do to triage and deploy fixes at scale.

items.title: Gifts from Crows, a picture book about the girl the crows paid back
items.why: The true story of the Seattle girl whose dropped snacks earned her a steady supply of beads, buttons and trinkets from the neighbourhood crows is catnip for anyone who has watched corvids think. Now it is a children's picture book, and the review suggests it gets the birds right. Proof that crows keep accounts.
items.summary: 10,000 Birds reviews Gifts from Crows, a new children's picture book by Gideon Sterer from Clarion Books. It tells the true story of a young girl whose habit of dropping and later leaving food for local crows grew into a friendship in which the birds left her small objects in return.

items.title: 93 percent of paint splatters are valid Perl programs
items.why: A SIGBOVIK classic resurfacing to high votes, and deservedly so. The authors fed paint splatters through OCR and asked Perl to parse the result, and Perl, being Perl, accepted nearly all of it. The real joke is how little exaggeration it needed.
items.summary: A tongue-in-cheek paper from SIGBOVIK, the April Fools' research conference, ran images of paint splatters through optical character recognition and tested whether the resulting text parsed as Perl. Most of it did, and the paper presents a gallery of the prettiest examples and what they actually do.

items.title: The eight horses of King Mu, galloping across a silk scroll
items.why: King Mu of Zhou is the legendary ruler who rode his eight marvellous steeds to the edge of the world to visit the Queen Mother of the West. This scroll, from around 1300, shows the horses off duty and misbehaving, which is a nice change from the usual stately equine portrait. Zoom in and enjoy the attitude.
items.summary: The Public Domain Review presents a silk handscroll from around 1300 depicting the eight horses of King Mu, the mythical team that carried the Zhou king on his far-flung journeys. The painting shows the animals rolling, grazing and cavorting rather than posed for display.

items.title: Uranus and Neptune's lopsided magnetic fields may reshuffle themselves quickly
items.why: Everything we know firsthand about these fields comes from a single Voyager 2 flyby in the 1980s, which is a thin dataset to hang a planet's personality on. The fun twist is that the models suggest the fields shift fast enough that the next spacecraft may find something rather different, which is either an argument for an ice-giant orbiter or a very good excuse.
items.summary: Uranus and Neptune have magnetic fields that are tilted far from their spin axes and badly offset from their centres, unlike Earth's tidy dipole. New modelling of their unusual interiors suggests these messy fields may change on short timescales, so they could already look different from what Voyager 2 measured.

items.title: The SS United States, once the fastest liner afloat, goes down as the world's largest artificial reef
items.why: She still holds the transatlantic speed record from 1952 and spent decades rusting at a Philadelphia pier while people argued about what to do with her. A reef is a gentler ending than the scrapyard: tuna and divers get a very large, very fast-looking home, and the ship gets to stay whole.
items.summary: The SS United States, the ocean liner that set the transatlantic speed record, has been scuttled in the Gulf of Mexico off the Florida panhandle. The multimillion-dollar project turns her into what will be the largest artificial reef anywhere, aimed at divers, anglers and big pelagic fish.

items.title: Birds that got snubbed in their names
items.why: A follow-up to the flattering-names list, this time collecting the species that taxonomists clearly didn't warm to. The header bird is a Plain Prinia, which is a fine joke in itself, and anyone who has spent time sorting out Southeast Asian warblers will recognise the frustration behind some of these names.
items.summary: A light 10,000 Birds piece rounding up bird species whose common names are outright put-downs, from dull and plain to names suggesting the bird is barely worth describing. It pairs with an earlier list of species given glowing names.

items.title: Plumbers 2026: glibc's slow catch-up with system calls that have no wrapper
items.why: A year after raising the issue at Plumbers, the glibc maintainers came back with a progress report and questions for the room. Anyone who has shipped a new system call knows the awkward gap between the kernel merging it and libc users being able to call it without reaching for syscall(), and this is the follow-through on closing it.
items.summary: LWN reports on Carlos O'Donell and Florian Weimer's session at this year's Linux Plumbers Conference on Linux system calls that glibc still doesn't wrap, leaving programs to reach them through raw syscall(). They covered what has been added in the past year and asked attendees how to handle the remaining backlog.

items.title: Tim Peters, author of the Zen of Python and timsort, has died
items.why: Guido's remembrance is the kind of thing the old mailing-list days were made of: a mentor who showed up early, argued for int and float mixing because that is what users would expect, and stayed for decades. Timsort alone lives in more sort routines than most of us will ever touch, and the Zen of Python is still quoted at code reviews. Worth reading slowly.
items.summary: Guido van Rossum announced on the Python forums that Tim Peters died in July. Peters was an early and lasting influence on Python's design, wrote PEP 20 (the Zen of Python), and created the timsort algorithm used well beyond Python.

items.title: Voltage glitching a mining card's fuses turns it into a faster-than-retail A100
items.why: The headline trick is satisfying, but the real lesson is the design inversion: on this die, blowing more fuses can unlock features rather than lock them, which is the opposite of how one-time fuses are supposed to be used. Full-size hardware hacking with a good writeup, and the extra enabled SMs are a nice reminder of how much silicon ships switched off for yield.
items.summary: A hardware hacker used voltage fault injection on Nvidia's GA100 die to blow arbitrary fuses, converting a cut-down CMP 170HX mining card into the equivalent of a datacentre A100. With all working SMs enabled, the unlocked cards run around 20 percent faster than retail A100s, and features like NVLink look recoverable too.

items.title: The ugly, brilliant drawings of Urs Graf, mercenary and artist
items.why: Graf was a Swiss goldsmith who went to war as a mercenary and drew what he saw and did, without much interest in looking good. The Public Domain Review essay finds melancholy under the swagger, which is a more interesting read than the usual Renaissance-artist-was-a-scoundrel angle.
items.summary: A Public Domain Review essay by Miya Tokumitsu on Urs Graf the Elder, a sixteenth-century Swiss draughtsman who also fought as a mercenary. His pen drawings of soldiers, camp followers and battlefield misery are vivid and often grim, and the essay reads a weary sadness into them.

items.title: Cossit House, the oldest home in Sydney, Nova Scotia
items.why: A 1787 house built for the Loyalist chaplain of what was then the separate colony of Cape Breton, which is a piece of Canadian history most people never learn. It comes with the obligatory resident ghosts, but the more interesting haunting is the colony itself, swallowed back into Nova Scotia a few decades later.
items.summary: Cossit House, built in 1787 for the Anglican minister Ranna Cossit, is the oldest surviving house in Sydney and among the oldest buildings on Cape Breton Island. It is now a museum in the city's historic North End, with local tales of early residents who never quite moved out.

items.title: Revisiting Terry Gilliam's Brazil, Orwell by way of ductwork
items.why: Reactor's film club takes on the 1985 film where Nineteen Eighty-Four meets Monty Python's paperwork and somehow never feels dated. Kali Wallace is good on why the comedy makes the dystopia worse rather than lighter, and on the endless retro-futurist plumbing that makes the film look like nothing else.
items.summary: A Reactor Science Fiction Film Club column on Brazil, Terry Gilliam's satire of a bureaucratic retro-future co-written with Tom Stoppard and starring Jonathan Pryce. The piece looks at how it riffs on Orwell, its absurd humour, and its distinctive look.

items.title: How palaeontologists read the Ediacaran, where animals first learned to move
items.why: Not dinosaurs, but the deep prequel: the strange soft-bodied life of the Ediacaran, half a billion years ago, before anything had a skeleton. A short Aeon video, and the claim of the earliest known handedness in an animal is the hook worth sticking around for.
items.summary: A short Aeon video following a palaeontologist who studies Ediacaran fossils, among the earliest complex life on Earth. It shows how trace fossils reveal when animals began moving under their own power, and an early example of left- or right-handedness.

items.title: A hot Jupiter stops transiting, and a hidden neighbour takes the blame
items.why: Planets that vanish make for good headlines and bad physics, so it is nice to see the boring-but-correct explanation win: gravity from an unseen sibling. Seven years of TESS light curves is a long enough baseline to watch an orbit slowly tilt, which is the real treat here.
items.summary: TESS watched a hot Jupiter about a thousand light years away transit its star for seven years, then the transits stopped. Astronomers think an undetected giant companion has been tugging the planet's orbit until it no longer crosses the star from our point of view.

items.title: Chandra catches a supernova impostor feeding off a hidden companion
items.why: Luminous Blue Variables are the stars that keep faking their own deaths, flaring up like supernovae and then carrying on. Chandra's X-ray view suggests at least one of them does it on a schedule because a black hole or neutron star is stirring it, which turns a mystery into an orbital mechanics problem.
items.summary: Some massive stars produce outbursts bright enough to be mistaken for supernovae but survive to repeat them. New X-ray observations indicate that one such impostor is in a binary with a compact object, a black hole or neutron star, which would explain why its outbursts come periodically.

items.title: The gentoo penguin turns out to be four species, the first new penguin in a century
items.why: Nothing new was found on an ice floe; the discovery happened in the sequencer. Genetic work shows the bird everyone filed as one widespread gentoo is really four separate species, which is a quiet reminder of how much of the bird list is still being argued over.
items.summary: Scientists have used genetic evidence to show that the gentoo penguin, long treated as a single species across a wide range, is actually four distinct species. It is being described as the first new penguin species recognised in about a hundred years.

items.title: The Rough-legged Hawk, the late-season prize at the hawk watch
items.why: By mid-November the big raptor passage is over and the hawk watchers who stay out are holding on for visitors from the far north. A Rough-legged Hawk, legs feathered to the toes for Arctic weather, is the sort of bird that makes the cold worth it. Penang has no hawk watch quite like this, but any raptor fan knows the feeling.
items.summary: A 10,000 Birds post on the Rough-legged Hawk, an Arctic-breeding buzzard that turns up at North American hawk watches late in the autumn season. With most migrants already past, it is one of the infrequent northern raptors that keeps watchers out in November weather.

items.title: A bronze lamplighter, forever mid-climb, in a hidden courtyard in The Hague
items.why: Public sculpture usually stands on a plinth looking important; this one is caught halfway up a lamp post with his coat flapping. It is a small, cheerful thing to go and find in a quiet corner of The Hague, and a nod to a job that electricity quietly abolished.
items.summary: In the Mallemolen, a tucked-away cobbled court in The Hague, a bronze figure by Dutch sculptor Loek Bos clambers up a street lamp. Installed in 2008, The Lamplighter commemorates the workers who once lit the city's lamps by hand every evening.

items.title: Sub-Saharan Africa's cities are set to double again, and whether they bring prosperity is the open question
items.why: Timothy Taylor doing what he does well: one World Bank report, a few figures, no sermon. The arithmetic is the striking bit, since a city population that doubles needs jobs or productivity to double just to keep incomes flat, and Africa's urbanisation has not reliably come with growth the way East Asia's did.
items.summary: The Conversable Economist walks through a World Bank report on urbanisation in sub-Saharan Africa, where the urban population has grown more than fivefold since 1975 and could double again within about 25 years. The report asks whether these cities will become engines of growth or poverty traps, noting that the link between urbanisation and income there has been mixed.

items.title: Most catastrophic distributed-systems failures come from botched error handling, via The Morning Paper
items.why: A classic from OSDI 2014 that every on-call engineer should have tattooed somewhere: the worse the outage, the dumber the root cause. Adrian Colyer's write-up of the Yuan et al. study is a good excuse to reread the finding that a third of the system-killing bugs were visible to plain code review of error handlers.
items.summary: The Morning Paper summarises a study of 198 user-reported failures in Cassandra, HBase, HDFS, MapReduce and Redis. Almost all of the catastrophic ones came from mishandled non-fatal errors that the code had already signalled, many of them trivial, and the authors built a static checker to catch such patterns.

items.title: What if a process could ignore SIGKILL? Someone patched Linux to find out
items.why: This is pure late-night hacking in the best tradition: take the one rule everybody knows is absolute and see what breaks when you bend it. Worth reading for the tour of how the kernel delivers the two signals userland is never allowed to catch, and for whatever chaos follows.
items.summary: A blogger modifies the Linux kernel so that processes can handle or ignore SIGKILL and SIGSTOP, the two signals POSIX reserves as unstoppable. The post explains how signals are delivered and why these two are special, then explores what happens once the guarantee is gone.

items.title: Kensler's permute(): visiting an array in random order without shuffling it
items.why: A small, elegant trick from the rendering world: a hash-based permutation that gives you the i-th element of a pseudorandom ordering in constant time and no memory. The author is careful about what it is not (anything cryptographic), which makes it more trustworthy, not less.
items.summary: A write-up of Andrew Kensler's permute() function, popular in offline rendering, which maps an index to a unique position in a pseudorandom permutation of an array without storing any state. It lets you sample items without replacement or iterate in random order without a Fisher-Yates shuffle first.

items.title: A sprouting bean, a flamingo, and a photographer's book of unlikely twins
items.why: A calm one for an idle moment. Photographer Andrew Zuckerman noticed a bean's curve echoed a flamingo he had shot fifteen years earlier, then went through 25 years of his own archive looking for more pairs. The result is the kind of looking that makes you notice shapes on your next walk.
items.summary: Photographer Andrew Zuckerman spotted that a sprouting bean in his studio had the same curve as an old photo of a flamingo. Pairing the two set off a search through about 2,500 of his nature images from the past 25 years, which became his new book, United Nature.

items.title: A 450-million-year-old starfish relative, soft tissue and all, turns up in a museum drawer
items.why: Not a dinosaur, and older than the first one by a couple of hundred million years, but soft tissue that survives that long earns its slot. Note where it was found: not in a quarry but in a collection, which keeps happening and keeps being the best argument for funding museum basements.
items.summary: Researchers have described an Ordovician echinoderm, a distant relative of starfish, whose fossil preserves soft parts that normally rot long before anything can turn to stone. The specimen had been sitting in a museum collection, and its tissues give new evidence for how early reef-dwelling animals fed and lived.

items.title: A digital twin of Webb scrubs away starlight and finds a planet hiding in old data
items.why: The trick here is modelling the telescope itself so precisely that you can subtract its glare and see what was underneath all along. The pleasing bit is that the new planet was found in data that already existed; archival astronomy keeps paying dividends long after the observing run ends.
items.summary: Astronomers built a detailed simulation of the James Webb Space Telescope's optics and used it to remove the light of bright stars from images. The method makes faint exoplanets between two and fifteen times easier to spot than standard techniques, and it has already pulled one previously unnoticed planet out of existing observations.

items.title: London's parakeets, and the question of whether anyone wants tens of thousands of them
items.why: Kottke flags a piece with the best headline of the week, the Pollycrisis, about the feral parakeets that have made themselves at home in London. Anyone who birds in Penang knows what an introduced, noisy, very successful parrot looks like; it is oddly comforting to see another city wrestling with the same green question.
items.summary: A short pointer from Kottke to an article on London's large and growing population of feral parakeets, birds of South Asian origin that now squabble across the city's parks. The piece asks what, if anything, a city should do about an invasive species that many residents have come to enjoy.

items.title: Mark Erelli premieres 'Talking To A Hurricane', written with an Army veteran
items.why: Boston's own Mark Erelli, timed for Veterans Day, with a song co-written at a music therapy retreat in North Andover. Erelli plays nearly everything on it himself, which is the kind of one-man-band craftsmanship this feed quietly admires.
items.summary: Folk Alley premiered a new song from Boston-based songwriter Mark Erelli for Veterans Day. He wrote it with drummer and US Army veteran Jeremy Lyon at a Music Therapy Retreats session in Massachusetts, and Erelli handles vocals, guitars, mandolin, keys, bass and percussion on the recording.

items.title: Marvin the Mastodon, keeping watch over a Nova Scotia highway
items.why: Roadside giant statues are a noble tradition, and this one has a better excuse than most: the real thing turned up nearby. A quarry operator spotted a tusk in a sinkhole in 1991, which beats anything most of us have found at work.
items.summary: At Mastodon Ridge in Stewiacke, Nova Scotia, a life-size mastodon statue about four metres tall stands above the highway. It went up in 1995 to mark the discovery a few years earlier of two mastodon skeletons, an adult and a juvenile, in a sinkhole at a gypsum quarry near Milford.

items.title: Twenty years of Linux route lookup performance, and the regression that ate the gains
items.why: Vincent Bernat updates his long-running IPv4 and IPv6 route lookup benchmarks all the way to 7.3, on a pinned Zen 4c box with one compiler for every kernel. The fun part is watching years of careful wins, from the RCU conversion to the removal of indirect calls, get wiped out by a single 200 ns regression in 6.5, and then the hunt for who did it.
items.summary: A benchmark study of how fast the Linux kernel resolves IPv4 and IPv6 routes across many releases, extending earlier measurements up to Linux 7.3. It credits the changes that sped lookups up over the years and traces a large slowdown introduced in Linux 6.5 to its source.

items.title: Hitchhiker: cheaper erasure-code repairs, via The Morning Paper
items.why: This week's dip into the Morning Paper archive is Rashmi et al.'s Hitchhiker, which tackles the dirty secret of Reed-Solomon in HDFS: rebuilding one lost block means reading a whole stripe's worth of data. The towel is optional, but the network savings are not.
items.summary: Adrian Colyer's 2014 write-up of a paper on erasure coding in large storage clusters. Hitchhiker layers a cheap transformation on top of Reed-Solomon codes so that repairing a lost block needs noticeably less disk reading and network traffic, without giving up the storage savings or fault tolerance.

items.title: Taking apart Star Wars Episode I: Racer's multiplayer, down to a remote code exec
items.why: A 1999 LAN game, DirectPlay, Wireshark and a homemade dissector: this is reverse engineering as a hobby in the best sense. The bug itself matters less than the tour of how late-90s games talked to each other over UDP.
items.summary: Researchers at Synacktiv dissected the local network protocol of the 1999 LucasArts game Star Wars Episode I: Racer. They wrote a Wireshark dissector, built tools around DirectPlay, and found a flaw that lets a malicious player run code on another machine.

items.title: Sara Weiss's 1903 Journeys to the Planet Mars, spiritualism with a spaceship's itinerary
items.why: Long before anyone claimed to have been taken aboard a saucer, people were travelling to Mars by trance. The Public Domain Review makes the case that this odd book is a missing link between the seance parlour and the UFO abductee, which is a lovely bit of cultural archaeology for any SF reader.
items.summary: A Public Domain Review piece on a 1903 book by Sara Weiss describing her spirit journeys to Mars and the beings she said she met there. The essay places it as a bridge between Victorian Spiritualism and the flying-saucer encounter stories of the next century.

items.title: Type in any place and see every satellite that passed over it this week, with its photos
items.why: A weekend project from a self-described satellite nerd that propagates the whole CelesTrak catalogue in the browser and then fetches real Sentinel-2 and Landsat frames from those passes. The detail worth noticing: Sentinel timestamps can be minutes off from the actual overflight, so some careful orbital arithmetic went into lining them up.
items.summary: A Show HN web app that, for any location, lists the satellites that flew overhead in the past seven days and shows actual imagery those satellites captured. It tracks more than seventeen thousand orbiting objects with SGP4, drawing them all on the GPU, and runs in the browser.

items.title: 35-million-year-old teeth from Thailand reveal a rodent the size of a large dog
items.why: Not a dinosaur, but palaeontology from practically next door, which counts double. Researchers have read a body mass of roughly thirty kilos off a handful of molars, which is a reminder of how much a good tooth can tell you. Somewhere in Westley's fire swamp, a rodent of unusual size nods knowingly.
items.summary: Fossil teeth dug up in Thailand belong to an extinct rodent from the late Eocene, around 35 million years ago. From the size of the teeth, researchers estimate the animal weighed about as much as a big dog, putting it in capybara territory and far from the giant South American rodents people usually picture.

items.title: Thirty years of curl, from a hundred-line download tool to everywhere
items.why: Daniel Stenberg marks the anniversary of the tiny HTTP fetcher that became curl, a project that probably runs on more devices than any of us can count. It is the late-90s open source story in its purest form: someone posts a small useful thing, someone else picks it up, and three decades of quiet maintenance follow. Raise a glass to the plumbing.
items.summary: On 11 November 1996 a Brazilian student posted httpget, a bare-bones download tool of about a hundred lines of C. Daniel Stenberg found it days later, started contributing, and eventually turned it into curl. His anniversary post looks back on how the project grew and what it took to keep it going.

items.title: How LEGO instructions evolved, from box-art inspiration to step-by-step booklets
items.why: Every AFOL has an opinion on instruction booklets, from the sparse early sheets to today's call-out boxes and part counts. This is a short history of how LEGO taught people to build, and it quietly doubles as a history of technical illustration. Bonus points for noticing when the little arrows arrived.
items.summary: A brief history of LEGO building instructions since 1955. Before then, sets came with nothing more than pictures on the packaging for inspiration; the piece traces how that turned into the numbered, wordless booklets builders know today.

items.title: MeerKLASS makes the first direct measurement of how cosmic hydrogen clusters
items.why: Mapping the universe by the faint radio glow of neutral hydrogen has been promised for years, and this is a real step towards it. The trick is pulling a weak signal out of a sky full of much louder foregrounds, which is the radio astronomer's version of hearing a whisper at a rock concert. Expect the phrase intensity mapping to come up a lot.
items.summary: The MeerKLASS collaboration, using South Africa's MeerKAT telescope, reports the first direct detection of the large-scale clustering of neutral hydrogen gas. The technique could let astronomers map the structure of the universe over huge volumes without having to catalogue individual galaxies.

items.title: Israel Putnam's tombstone in Brooklyn, Connecticut
items.why: Old Put is the general of wolf-den and don't-fire-till-you-see-the-whites-of-their-eyes fame, depending on which legend you favour. His grave in a quiet corner of eastern Connecticut is just the kind of New England detour that rewards a slow drive. Bring a thermos and a sense of local legend.
items.summary: Atlas Obscura visits the memorial to Israel Putnam in Brooklyn, Connecticut. Putnam fought in the French and Indian War, became one of the Continental Army's first major generals in 1775 and led New England militia early in the Revolutionary War.

items.title: The Seoul Report: where systems research thinks it should go next
items.why: The first SIGOPS Strategic Workshop, held alongside SOSP 2025, produced a community report on the field's long-standing problems and its new ones. Worth reading for the old-guard complaints as much as the shiny agenda; the list of things OS people still can't do well has a familiar ring. Pour coffee, skip the abstract.
items.summary: A report from the first ACM SIGOPS Strategic Workshop, held with SOSP 2025 in Seoul. Organisers and participants summarise discussions on lasting operating systems challenges and on what specialised hardware, AI and very large infrastructure change for the field.

items.title: Gray on lock granularity and degrees of consistency, via The Morning Paper
items.why: Jim Gray's 1975 paper is where hierarchical locking and intention modes come from, and it still reads like a design review you wish you had been in. Adrian Colyer's write-up walks both halves: overhead versus concurrency, then consistency versus concurrency. Anyone who has stared at a lock hierarchy in a kernel will feel at home.
items.summary: An archive post from The Morning Paper's series on database techniques everyone should know. It covers Gray and colleagues' 1975 paper on lock granularity, which weighs locking cost against concurrency, and on degrees of consistency, the ancestors of today's isolation levels.

items.title: D. W. Griffith's A Corner in Wheat, a 1909 short on cornering the grain market
items.why: Before the epics and the controversies, Griffith made this lean little film about a speculator who corners wheat while farmers and bread queues pay the price. Its cross-cutting between the trading floor and the breadline is a famous early bit of film grammar. About a quarter of an hour, public domain, and surprisingly sharp.
items.summary: The Public Domain Review presents A Corner in Wheat, a 1909 short by D. W. Griffith. It tells a moral tale of a speculator's greed in the grain trade, drawing on Frank Norris's novels about monopoly and the wheat business.

items.title: John Barnes's In the Hall of the Martian King, the end of the Jak Jinnaka trilogy
items.why: Alan Brown's column on classic adventure SF reaches the last book of Barnes's often overlooked young-adult trilogy. Barnes is the author of Mother of Storms and A Million Open Doors, and even his lighter work tends to have sharp edges. A good nudge to dig out a series that slipped past many readers.
items.summary: A review of In the Hall of the Martian King, the third and final book in John Barnes's Jak Jinnaka series, part of Reactor's regular column revisiting classic science fiction about soldiers, spacers and explorers.

items.title: The US Postal Service will issue mythical creature stamps in 2027
items.why: Five cryptids are getting stamps, Mothman among them, which means the Point Pleasant legend is now official enough to mail a utility bill with. There is something cheerful about a postal service leaning into folklore. The truth is out there, and it costs one first-class rate.
items.summary: The USPS has revealed part of its 2027 stamp programme, including a Mythical Creatures set of five cryptids. Mothman, first reported around Point Pleasant, West Virginia, in 1966, is the youngest legend of the bunch.

items.title: A new iguanodontian from the Sussex mud, filed as Iguanodon for 25 years
items.why: Second museum-drawer dinosaur in two runs, which says something about how much is still sitting in collections waiting for a second look. The name is the fun part: a marsh-dwelling hadrosaur relative, which is about as close as the English Wealden gets to a swamp-thing tribute.
items.summary: Palaeontologists have described Paludohadros proudlovii, a plant-eating iguanodontian that lived in the wetlands of southern England around 125 million years ago. Its bones, dug from a brickworks, spent roughly a quarter of a century in the Natural History Museum's collections lumped in with Iguanodon before a closer look showed a new species with an unusually shaped snout.

items.title: Sarah Jarosz plays the Colonial Theatre in Bethlehem, New Hampshire, on Friday
items.why: A favourite artist in a century-old small-town theatre in the White Mountains, billed as a ten-years-of-Undercurrent show, which is about as New England a night out as the folk circuit offers. Worth noting for anyone tracking her solo dates between I'm With Her runs.
items.summary: Sarah Jarosz is booked into the Colonial Theatre in Bethlehem, New Hampshire, on November 13, a show marking ten years since her Grammy-winning album Undercurrent. The local paper in Vermont's Northeast Kingdom flagged the date for its readers.

items.title: Punch Brothers and Jeff Tweedy team up for a seven-city PB&J tour in February
items.why: Chris Thile's string band and the Wilco frontman co-headlining is the sort of crossover that sounds odd on paper and probably isn't: both camps worship a well-built song. The hook is that they plan to play each other's material, so expect Tweedy tunes with a banjo-and-fiddle rethink.
items.summary: Punch Brothers and Jeff Tweedy will share the bill on a short co-headlining run, billed as the PB&J tour, through seven cities in the eastern and southern United States in February. The pairing promises sets where each act takes on the other's songs.

items.title: Why red giants hiccup on their way up: a fresh explanation for the RGB bump
items.why: A neat old puzzle: as a Sun-like star swells into a red giant it brightens steadily, except for one short stretch where it briefly dims before carrying on. Astronomers use that bump as a calibration point, so a cleaner account of what causes it is worth more than it sounds.
items.summary: When low-mass stars leave the main sequence and climb the red giant branch, their brightness rises steadily apart from a brief dip known as the RGB luminosity bump. An astrophysicist has proposed a new explanation for the dip, which has long resisted a fully satisfying account.

items.title: The new Grimmett and Inskipp guide to the birds of the Indian Subcontinent, reviewed
items.why: A field guide review by a birder who wore out the first edition in Nepal and India, which is the only kind of field guide review worth reading. The Helm guides are the ones that end up dog-eared in a backpack, and the second edition is the update a lot of regional birders have been waiting on since 2011.
items.summary: A detailed review of the second edition of Birds of the Indian Subcontinent, the Helm field guide by Richard Grimmett, Carol Inskipp and Tim Inskipp. The book covers India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan and the Maldives, a region holding something like an eighth of the world's bird species, and the reviewer walks through what has changed since the 2011 edition.

items.title: The Bundesbüdchen, the kiosk that fed West Germany's politicians in Bonn
items.why: When Bonn unexpectedly became the provisional capital, it had Beethoven's birthplace and not much in the way of lunch. A family kiosk filled the gap and became part of the furniture of the Bonn Republic, which is the best kind of footnote to postwar history.
items.summary: In 1949 the small university town of Bonn was chosen as West Germany's provisional seat of government, but it had little to offer hungry officials. In 1957 the Rausch family set up a small kiosk near the government quarter, and the Bundesbüdchen, the federal kiosk, became a fixture where ministers, staff and journalists grabbed snacks between sessions.

items.title: Goethe and Schiller's Xenions, a book-length exercise in literary insult
items.why: Two giants of German letters teaming up to write hundreds of barbed couplets about their critics and rivals is the eighteenth-century version of a subtweet storm, only in elegiac metre. The 1896 edition is a handsome thing to browse even if your German stops at Kindergarten.
items.summary: The Public Domain Review presents an 1896 edition of the Xenien, the collection of satirical epigrams Goethe and Schiller wrote together in the 1790s to skewer the literary figures and critics of their day. It ranks among the most elaborate collaborative works of literary mockery ever published.

items.title: LWN on the first part of the Linux 7.4 merge window
items.why: Now out from behind the paywall: Jon Corbet's first tour through what landed for 7.4. The interesting aside is the talk of stretching the merge window to three weeks, which tells you something about how the maintainer pipeline is coping these days.
items.summary: LWN's first merge-window report for Linux 7.4 covers the 6,753 non-merge changesets pulled into mainline in its opening stretch, with many more expected and a possible extension of the window to three weeks. It summarises the notable new features alongside the ongoing cleanup and security work.

items.title: The hardest tarball: one archive that extracts eight different ways
items.why: A single GNU tar command, a hard link renamed to a name with an accented letter, and a pax header that claims a size it shouldn't: the result is an archive every extractor reads differently. A lovely bit of format archaeology, and a quiet reminder that tar has never really been one format.
items.summary: A short write-up of a curious tar archive that unpacks in eight distinct ways depending on which tool opens it. It works by abusing how a pax extended header can override the size of a hard-link entry, so that different implementations disagree about where the next header begins.

items.title: Tiny Valencia: the whole city as an isometric SimCity-style pixel map
items.why: Someone painted all of Valencia, from the huerta to the Albufera lagoon, in the style of a 90s city builder, and every building is a real one. A pleasant place to get lost for ten minutes, and a map lover's idea of a screensaver.
items.summary: Tiny Valencia is a zoomable isometric pixel-art map of the Spanish city, built by rendering real 3D cadastral and terrain data from a fixed angle and then repainting it tile by tile in a consistent pixel style. It covers almost the entire municipality, including the port and the Albufera.

items.title: A new tapejarid pterosaur, hiding in a Cambridge drawer since 1870
items.why: The best fossil hunting this year keeps happening indoors: a scrap described in the reign of Victoria turns out to be a whole new genus once someone looks at it with modern eyes. Tapejarids are the crested, toothless show-offs of the pterosaur world, mostly known from Brazil and China, so one turning up in an English collection is the bit worth noticing.
items.summary: Palaeontologists have named a new genus and species of tapejarid pterosaur, Hintighernia edingerae, from a specimen held at the Sedgwick Museum of Earth Sciences in Cambridge. The bone was first written up in 1870 and sat in the collection for more than a century and a half before being re-examined.

items.title: Punch Brothers at DC's Warner Theatre, reviewed
items.why: Favourite-band rule applies, and gladly: a second dispatch from the current Punch Brothers tour, this time from the Washington leg a few days before their Connecticut stop. Read it for a fresh pair of ears on how Thile and company are stretching the material live.
items.summary: A live review of Punch Brothers' 6 November show at the Warner Theatre in Washington, DC, written up by the local music site Parklife DC.

items.title: Perseverance has been quietly testing spacesuit fabric against Martian dust
items.why: One of the less glamorous passengers on Perseverance is a set of spacesuit material swatches, sitting out in the weather so future astronauts don't have to find out the hard way. Dust is the problem nobody puts on the mission poster, and here's someone actually measuring it.
items.summary: Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis studied how Martian dust settles on and interacts with the spacesuit material samples carried on the Perseverance rover's calibration target. The results feed into planning for crewed missions, where dust exposure will wear on both people and equipment.

items.title: A millisecond pulsar caught just as it finished eating its companion
items.why: Pulsar recycling is usually a story told from the before and the after; this pair seems to have been spotted right at the moment the meal ended, with crumbs still floating around. A nice snapshot of a stage of stellar evolution that should be brief and rarely seen.
items.summary: Millisecond pulsars get their speed by pulling mass and spin from a companion star, which in turn is hurried along towards becoming a white dwarf. Astronomers have found a pulsar whose white dwarf companion looks to have only just finished that transfer, with leftover debris still visible around the system.

items.title: Building an open source network switch, one free chip tapeout at a time
items.why: Someone decided the way to own their networking gear was to start at the silicon, and then actually did it: first a tiny three-port switch on Tiny Tapeout, now a shot at a whole chip of their own. This is the late-90s spirit in its purest form, with a deadline and a lot of adrenaline.
items.summary: A hobbyist on a long-running quest to build open source networking hardware, ending eventually in a full router, writes up designing a switch ASIC. After an earlier three-port switch went out on a shared Tiny Tapeout run, a chance came up to tape out a complete chip for free, with some tight constraints to work around.

items.title: The Jurassic Jungle Boat Ride, Pigeon Forge's gloriously terrible attraction
items.why: Every roadside strip needs a ride so bad it becomes a pilgrimage, and the Smoky Mountains have this one, tucked a stone's throw from Dollywood. The mannequin queue out front is the detail that sells it: even the crowd is fake.
items.summary: A small indoor dinosaur boat ride in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, wedged among the independent tourist attractions near Dollywood. Theme park fans have long ranked it among the worst rides in the country, which has become its main draw, and the waiting line outside is made of mannequins.

items.title: Snail houses and mechanical flies from a 15th-century book of natural wonders
items.why: Before field guides there were books like this one, where a real snail and an invented marvel shared the same page with equal conviction. Robert Testard's illuminations are the draw: bright, odd and very sure of themselves.
items.summary: The Public Domain Review looks at Robert Testard's illustrations for Les secretz de l'histoire naturelle, an illuminated manuscript from around 1485. The book collects the marvels of the known world and beyond, from snails and bog bodies to mechanical flies.

items.title: David Bratman, Tolkien scholar and fandom stalwart, has died
items.why: Bratman was one of those people who made the Tolkien and Inklings corner of scholarship a friendlier, sharper place, and he also did the thankless arithmetic of running the Hugos three times. Mike Glyer's tribute is a good way to remember the fannish side of serious criticism.
items.summary: File 770 marks the death on 9 November of David Bratman at 69. He was a scholar of Tolkien and the Inklings, a longtime fanzine writer and a three-time Hugo Awards administrator, remembered for a careful analytical mind and a gift for writing.

items.title: Jacobson and Karels on congestion avoidance, via The Morning Paper
items.why: The paper everyone cites and fewer have reread: the 1986 collapse that shrank a 400-yard link to 40 bps, and the slow-start and backoff machinery that came out of it. Adrian Colyer's write-up is a good excuse to notice how much of today's retry and circuit-breaker folklore is just Jacobson rediscovered.
items.summary: An archive post from The Morning Paper on Van Jacobson and Michael Karels's classic congestion avoidance work, prompted by the internet's congestion collapses of the mid-1980s. It walks through their fixes for TCP and argues the same ideas apply wherever traffic and backoff have to be managed.

items.title: Foldable Flight, a whole site of serious paper airplanes
items.why: A thousand-odd upvotes for paper airplanes is the most wholesome thing that's happened on that site all week. Behind the folding diagrams there's real aerodynamics, plus the design lineage of a world-record glider, and it costs one sheet of printer paper to try.
items.summary: Foldable Flight is a collection of paper airplane designs with folding tutorials, from simple darts to fighter-inspired models, flapping gliders and the prototype of a record-breaking design. Some designs can also take small add-on motors.

items.title: M. John Harrison wins the 2026 Booker Prize
items.why: The man who spent decades taking the spaceship-and-ray-gun furniture of the genre apart has now walked off with the most establishment prize in British letters. Harrison was always the New Wave writer other writers whispered about, the Light and Kefahuchi Tract crowd's patron saint of the unknowable. A nice moment for anyone who's ever had to defend SF at a dinner party.
items.summary: British science fiction writer M. John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize for The End of Everything, his thirteenth novel, a dystopian satire about how little humans can actually understand. The award comes with fifty thousand pounds.

items.title: A fossil pygmy sperm whale from Peru with the most lopsided face on record
items.why: No dinosaurs in the pool this time, so here's palaeontology's next best thing: a six-million-year-old whale that looks like it was assembled by a committee. Toothed whales are already asymmetric in the skull thanks to their echolocation plumbing, but this one takes it to an extreme. Peru's Pisco coast keeps turning up marine oddities like this.
items.summary: Researchers have described a pygmy sperm whale skull from Late Miocene rocks in southern Peru whose facial bones are more asymmetric than in any known whale, living or extinct. The animal had a downturned snout and probably foraged along the shallow sea floor, a lifestyle unlike its modern relatives.

items.title: Mars may still have magma chambers after all
items.why: Mars is usually filed as a geologically retired planet, but the Trace Gas Orbiter keeps catching whiffs of hydrogen chloride at times of year when nothing but volcanic outgassing explains it well. Add some freshly spotted fissures as a possible source and the case for a faintly warm interior gets more interesting. Worth watching for the inevitable rebuttal paper.
items.summary: New research argues that pockets of magma may persist beneath the Martian surface. ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter detected hydrogen chloride, a gas tied to volcanic activity, in a season when other explanations struggle, and the team identified new surface fissures that could be venting it.

items.title: 568 currencies since 1850, and what happened to the 405 that died
items.why: Timothy Taylor at his best: one new dataset, a couple of charts, and no axe to grind. The rise and fall of the world's currencies traces the end of empires, the spread of independence across Africa and Asia, and the Soviet breakup in a single line graph. A reminder that money is far more mortal than it looks in your wallet.
items.summary: The Conversable Economist walks through a new Bank for International Settlements working paper that catalogues every currency issued worldwide since 1850. Of 568 currencies, 405 have been discontinued; the post charts how the total grew with decolonisation and jumped again when the Soviet Union dissolved.

items.title: Kathmandu's day of the crow, and the man who holds a Crow Conference
items.why: Nepal sets aside a festival day to honour crows, and one folk singer has spent two decades calling them in with his own voice. The piece is also honest about the strain: urban crows and people don't always get along, and the old reverence sits uneasily beside modern complaints. Corvid behaviour, folklore and a microphone in one story.
items.summary: During Kaag Tihar, Nepal's annual crow day within the Diwali-season festival, Kathmandu folk singer and activist Ramesh Dulal hosts a gathering he calls the Crow Conference, mimicking calls to draw the birds in. Mongabay looks at the tradition and at the increasingly mixed relationship between the city's people and its house crows.

items.title: Turning an old LG phone into a wideband SDR without extra hardware
items.why: The recent trend of coaxing raw baseband samples out of cheap radio chips reaches its logical conclusion: a rooted budget Android phone that's now a software-defined receiver. A decade-old handset with LineageOS and some modem firmware spelunking does what used to need a dongle. Very much the spirit of using what's in the drawer.
items.summary: Hacker Logan Zarov converted an LG D325 Android phone into a wideband software-defined radio receiver with only minor modification, by getting at the modem's baseband data. The rooted phone runs LineageOS, and the project builds on recent work unlocking SDR capability in Wi-Fi, LoRa and microcontroller radio chips.

items.title: Willi Carlisle's 'The Universal Bubba', a record for the people who hold things together
items.why: Carlisle is one of the more interesting voices in the American folk revival, a squeezebox-and-banjo storyteller with a theatre background. This album grew from watching his grandmother keep a whole family running, which is about as folk a premise as they come. No Depression calls it hefty and rollicking, both of which suit a long November evening.
items.summary: No Depression profiles folk singer-songwriter Willi Carlisle and his new album The Universal Bubba, a celebration of everyday doers and builders. The title idea came from his grandmother, whose cooking, caretaking and constant work held the family together.

items.title: OpenBenches hits back at the scrapers with a blunt bot banhammer
items.why: A hobby site that maps memorial benches shouldn't be pushing terabytes a month, yet here we are. Terence Eden's answer is a delightfully crude trap that bans anything ignoring robots.txt, built to work even behind heavy caching, with a frank discussion of what it might break. Small web, defending itself.
items.summary: Terence Eden found that his volunteer project OpenBenches, a crowdsourced map of memorial benches, served over 2.5 terabytes in a month, mostly to AI crawlers. He describes a simple tool that catches and blocks bots which ignore the site's crawl rules, how to build one yourself, and the trade-offs involved.

items.title: Halifax's Drunken Lampposts
items.why: Public art with a sense of humour: a cluster of streetlights on the Halifax waterfront that appear to have overdone it at the pub. The official titles are even better than the nickname. The sort of thing you'd stumble across after a plate of fish and chips and need a second look at.
items.summary: On the Halifax waterfront in Nova Scotia, artists Chris Hanson and Hendrika Sonnenberg, both NSCAD University alumni, bent ordinary lampposts into slumped, staggering figures. The pieces poke fun at late-night behaviour in the city's bar district and have become a local landmark.

items.title: An alphametic with 41 addends that you shouldn't try to solve
items.why: Cryptarithms usually stop at SEND + MORE = MONEY. This one strings together a whole rambling sentence about a man trying to meet a team on the moon, and somehow every letter still maps to a single consistent digit. Futility Closet kindly prints the answer, which is the only sane approach.
items.summary: Futility Closet shares a huge letter-arithmetic puzzle devised by Anton Pavlis of Guelph, Ontario, in which 41 words are added together to spell TESTS. Each letter stands for one digit throughout, and the post gives the full numeric solution.

items.title: Punch Brothers bring the instrumental tour home to Storrs
items.why: Another stop on the autumn run, and the student paper at UConn came away calling it stellar. Thile and company have been touring without the vocals this time around, which in a room like the Jorgensen means five people having a long, intricate conversation on strings. It's the closest New England has to a home game for them.
items.summary: The UConn Daily Campus reviews Punch Brothers' November 7 concert at the Jorgensen Center for the Performing Arts in Storrs, Connecticut. The student reviewer rates the show highly, the latest leg of the band's autumn tour.

items.title: A Caltech robot assembles part of a structure in orbit, unsupervised
items.why: Every big space telescope so far has had to be folded like origami to fit inside a fairing. A robot that can put the pieces together once it's up there removes that ceiling entirely, and doing it autonomously means nobody on the ground has to fly every bolt. Small step, but the right direction.
items.summary: A Caltech-built robot has autonomously assembled part of a structure in space, which the team describes as a first. The aim is to eventually build large telescopes, antennas and solar power arrays in orbit, far bigger than anything a rocket could carry in one piece.

items.title: Lecithin, the stuff in your chocolate bar, might fix gel rocket fuel
items.why: Gel propellants promise the best of solids and liquids and tend to deliver the headaches of both. Two Concordia researchers reached into the food pantry for an emulsifier and report it smooths over some of those problems. There's something pleasing about rocketry borrowing a trick from mayonnaise.
items.summary: Researchers at Concordia University report in the journal Langmuir that lecithin, a common food emulsifier, can address several known problems with gelled rocket propellants. Gels sit between solid and liquid fuels and aim to combine the strengths of each, but have been tricky to handle in practice.

items.title: Two monarchs of Raja Ampat, and a scientific name you mustn't joke about
items.why: Raja Ampat is about as close to Penang's birding neighbourhood as 10,000 Birds gets, and monarch flycatchers are among the region's sharpest-dressed residents. The post opens by pre-emptively scolding anyone tempted by the Frilled Monarch's genus name, which is a fine way to start any bird write-up.
